title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 841–843 (Night 188, continuing nights-187), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 188 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Furious, the prince accuses the vizier of having coached the servant and demands to know where the girl who slept in his arms has gone. The vizier swears that no one was sent to him, that the door was locked all night, and suggests he dreamed it, from eating many kinds of food or the whispering of devils. Enraged, Qamar al-Zamān seizes him by his long beard, drags him off the couch and beats him half to death. Reasoning that if the servant saved himself with a lie he may do the same, the vizier pretends that the king made him keep the girl secret. The prince declares that if his father arranged all this to test him, he now consents to marry, and wants only that girl; he sends the vizier to his father for an answer, and the old man stumbles from the tower in terror to King Shahramān. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-thamānūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth and-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eighty-eighth night,
sentences.n: al-thāmina, “the eighth”, agrees with al-layla, and the tens, al-thamānūna, follow in the same nominative case. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا سَمِعَ كَلَامَ الْوَزِيرِ اغْتَاظَ غَيْظًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā samiʿa kalāma al-wazīri ightāẓa ghayẓan shadīdan
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, when he-heard (the) words (of) the-vizier, was-enraged a-rage severe.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Qamar al-Zamān heard what the vizier said, he flew into a violent rage.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the story by going back over the last moment of the night before: the vizier has just told Qamar al-Zamān what the servant reported of him. anna Qamara al-Zamāni … ightāẓa: the name comes first as the noun of anna, and the lammā clause sits between it and its verb. ightāẓa ghayẓan shadīdan, “he raged a fierce rage”, the cognate accusative: the verb repeated as a noun to say how hard.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لِلْوَزِيرِ تَبَيَّنَ لِي أَنَّكُمْ عَلَّمْتُمُ الْخَادِمَ الْفِعْلَ الَّذِي صَدَرَ مِنْهُ وَمَنَعْتُمُوهُ مِنْ أَنْ يُخْبِرَنِي بِأَمْرِ الصَّبِيَّةِ الَّتِي كَانَتْ نَائِمَةً عِنْدِي فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla li-al-wazīri tabayyana lī annakum ʿallamtumu al-khādima al-fiʿla alladhī ṣadara minhu wa-manaʿtumūhu min an yukhbiranī bi-amri al-ṣabiyyati allatī kānat nāʾimatan ʿindī fī hādhihi al-laylati
sentences.l: Then he-said to-the-vizier: It-has-become-clear to-me that-you (pl.) taught the-servant the-deed that issued from-him, and-you-prevented-him from that he-tell-me with-(the)-matter (of) the-girl who was sleeping with-me in this the-night.
sentences.i: Then he said to the vizier, “It is plain to me that you people put the servant up to what he did, and kept him from telling me about the girl who was sleeping with me this night.
sentences.n: The first half repeats, almost word for word, what the prince said as the last night ended; then he goes on. manaʿa min, “to prevent from”: min an yukhbiranī, “from telling me”, with the subjunctive after an. Before an object suffix the -tum of the verb lengthens to -tumū: manaʿtumūhu, “you prevented him”. akhbara bi-, “to tell of”: the verb takes the thing told with bi-, here amr, “the matter, the affair” of the girl. nāʾimatan, “sleeping”, is the predicate of kānat, in the accusative; its ئ is printed, as are the shaddas of تبيّن, علّمتم and الصبيّة. fī hādhihi al-layla, “this night”, means the night just past: the prince says it of that night again and again.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ أَعْقَلُ مِنَ الْخَادِمِ فَأَخْبِرْنِي فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ أَيْنَ ذَهَبَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ الَّتِي كَانَتْ نَائِمَةً فِي حِضْنِي تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ
sentences.tr: wa-anta ayyuhā al-wazīru aʿqalu mina al-khādimi fa-akhbirnī fī hādhihi al-sāʿati ayna dhahabati al-ṣabiyyatu allatī kānat nāʾimatan fī ḥiḍnī tilka al-laylata
sentences.l: And-you, O vizier, (are) more-sensible than the-servant; so-tell-me in this the-hour where went the-girl who was sleeping in my-bosom that the-night.
sentences.i: You, vizier, have more sense than the servant: so tell me, here and now, where the girl has gone who lay asleep in my arms that night.
sentences.n: aʿqal, “more sensible”, the elative of ʿāqil, with min, “than”. fī hādhihi al-sāʿa, “in this hour”, means “at once, right now”, a phrase the story leans on. ḥiḍn, “bosom, embrace”: fī ḥiḍnī, “in my arms”. tilka al-laylata, “that night”, an adverbial accusative of time. The shadda of ايّها is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَنْتُمُ الَّذِينَ أَرْسَلْتُمُوهَا عِنْدِي وَأَمَرْتُمُوهَا أَنْ تَنَامَ فِي حِضْنِي وَنِمْتُ وَإِيَّاهَا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ فَلَمَّا انْتَبَهْتُ مَا وَجَدْتُهَا فَأَيْنَ هِيَ الْآنَ
sentences.tr: fa-antumu alladhīna arsaltumūhā ʿindī wa-amartumūhā an tanāma fī ḥiḍnī wa-nimtu wa-iyyāhā ilā al-ṣabāḥi fa-lammā intabahtu mā wajadtuhā fa-ayna hiya al-āna
sentences.l: For-you (pl.) (are) the-ones-who sent-her to-me and-ordered-her that she-sleep in my-bosom; and-I-slept, and-her (with me), until the-morning; and-when I-woke, not I-found-her. So-where (is) she now?
sentences.i: It was you who sent her to me and told her to sleep in my arms, and I slept with her until morning; but when I woke I could not find her. So where is she now?”
sentences.n: antumu alladhīna, “you are the ones who”, with a helping -u on antum before the joining alif. arsala ʿinda, “to send to”, with ʿinda where Classical Arabic would say ilā, a later usage. nimtu wa-iyyāhā, “I slept, and she with me”: the wāw of accompaniment with the free-standing object pronoun iyyā-. intabaha, Form VIII, “to wake”. mā wajadtuhā, “I did not find her”, mā with the perfect for the past denial. The hamza and madda of الآن are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ يَاسَيِّدِي قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ اسْمُ اللَّهِ حَوَالَيْكَ وَاللَّهِ مَا أَرْسَلْنَالَكَ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ أَحَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru yā sayyidī Qamara al-Zamāni ismu Allāhi ḥawālayka wa-Allāhi mā arsalnā laka fī hādhihi al-laylati aḥadan
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-vizier: O-my-master Qamar al-Zamān, (the) name (of) God (be) around-you! By-God, not we-sent to-you in this the-night anyone.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “My master Qamar al-Zamān, God's name be about you! By God, we sent no one to you this night.
sentences.n: The print has نقال, a misprint for فقال, corrected here: fa-qāla, “so he said”. The print runs يا and سيدي together, ياسيدي; the spacing is kept. Qamara al-Zamāni stands beside sayyidī in the accusative of the one addressed. ismu Allāhi ḥawālayka, “the name of God be round about you”, a formula to ward off harm, said to a man who seems to be possessed: God's name is set about him like a wall. ḥawālay, “around”, is a dual form of ḥawl; the fatḥa on its lām is printed. The print also runs ارسلنا and لك together, ارسلنالك, read arsalnā laka, “we sent to you”; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ نِمْتَ وَحْدَكَ وَالْبَابُ مَقْفُولٌ عَلَيْكَ وَالْخَادِمُ نَائِمٌ مِنْ خَلْفِ الْبَابِ وَمَا أَتَى إِلَيْكَ صَبِيَّةٌ وَلَا غَيْرُهَا فَثَبِّتْ عَقْلَكَ وَارْجِعْ إِلَيْهِ يَاسَيِّدِي وَلَاتَشْغَلْ خَاطِرَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qad nimta waḥdaka wa-al-bābu maqfūlun ʿalayka wa-al-khādimu nāʾimun min khalfi al-bābi wa-mā atā ilayka ṣabiyyatun wa-lā ghayruhā fa-thabbit ʿaqlaka wa-irjiʿ ilayhi yā sayyidī wa-lā tashghal khāṭiraka
sentences.l: And-you-have slept alone, and-the-door (was) locked on-you, and-the-servant sleeping from behind the-door; and-not came to-you a-girl nor other-than-her. So-make-firm your-mind, and-return to-it, O-my-master, and-not occupy your-thoughts.
sentences.i: You slept alone, with the door locked on you and the servant asleep outside it, and no girl came to you, nor anyone else. So steady your mind and come back to your senses, my master, and do not trouble your thoughts.”
sentences.n: The fatḥa of نمتَ is printed: nimta, “you slept”. maqfūl, “locked”, for Classical muqfal: as with maghlūq in the last night, the later language makes the participle from the plain verb qafala. min khalfi al-bābi, “behind the door”, that is, outside it. atā ilayka ṣabiyyatun: the verb stays masculine though its subject is feminine, as often when the two are parted. thabbit, Form II imperative, “make firm, steady”; its shadda is printed. irjiʿ ilayhi, “return to it”: the -hi takes up ʿaql, “mind”, so “come back to your senses”. The print runs لا and تشغل together, ولاتشغل; the spacing is kept. lā tashghal khāṭiraka, “do not trouble your mind”: khāṭir is the mind as the seat of passing thoughts and cares.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَقَدِ اغْتَاظَ مِنْ كَلَامِهِ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ إِنَّ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةَ مَعْشُوقَتِي وَهِيَ الْمَلِيحَةُ صَاحِبَةُ الْعُيُونِ السُّودِ وَالْخُدُودِ الْحُمْرِ الَّتِي عَانَقْتُهَا فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ بِطُولِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-qadi ightāẓa min kalāmihi ayyuhā al-wazīru inna tilka al-ṣabiyyata maʿshūqatī wa-hiya al-malīḥatu ṣāḥibatu al-ʿuyūni al-sūdi wa-al-khudūdi al-ḥumri allatī ʿānaqtuhā fī hādhihi al-laylati bi-ṭūlihā
sentences.l: So-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān, and-he-had become-enraged from his-words: O vizier, indeed that the-girl (is) my-beloved, and-she (is) the-lovely-one, (the) owner (of) the-eyes the-black and-the-cheeks the-red, whom I-embraced in this the-night with-its-length.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān, enraged at his words, said to him, “Vizier, that girl is my beloved: the lovely one with the black eyes and the red cheeks, whom I held in my arms this whole night through.”
sentences.n: wa-qadi ightāẓa, “being by now enraged”: the wāw of state with qad and the perfect; qad takes a helping -i before the joining alif. ṣāḥibat al-ʿuyūn, “owner of the eyes”, the usual way of saying “she of the … eyes”. sūd and ḥumr are the plurals of aswad, “black”, and aḥmar, “red”, agreeing with the plurals ʿuyūn, “eyes”, and khudūd, “cheeks”: a stock pair of a beauty's marks. ʿānaqa, Form III, “to embrace”. bi-ṭūlihā, “the whole length of it”: bi- of extent, and -hā takes up al-layla.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ الْوَزِيرُ مِنْ كَلَامِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَقَالَ لَهُ هَلْ أَنْتَ رَأَيْتَ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةَ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ بِعَيْنِكَ فِى الْيَقَظَةِ أَمْ فِى الْمَنَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-wazīru min kalāmi Qamari al-Zamāni wa-qāla lahu hal anta raʾayta tilka al-ṣabiyyata fī hādhihi al-laylati bi-ʿaynika fī al-yaqaẓati am fī al-manāmi
sentences.l: So-marvelled the-vizier from (the) words (of) Qamar al-Zamān, and-said to-him: (Is it that) you, you-saw that the-girl in this the-night with-your-eye, in the-waking or in the-sleep?
sentences.i: The vizier marvelled at Qamar al-Zamān's words, and said to him, “Did you see that girl last night with your own eyes, awake, or in a dream?”
sentences.n: taʿajjaba min, Form V, “to wonder at”: min gives the cause. hal anta raʾayta, “did you see”, with the pronoun put first for stress. hal … am, “… or …?”: Classical Arabic asks a choice with a- … am, and hal here is the later usage. yaqaẓa, “waking”, against manām, “sleep, a dream”. The hamza of رأيت is printed, and so is the ى of فى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَا أَيُّهَا الشَّيْخُ النَّحْسُ أَتَظُنُّ أَنِّي رَأَيْتُهَا بِأُذُنِي إِنَّمَا رَأَيْتُهَا بِعُيُونِي فِى الْيَقَظَةِ وَقَلَّبْتُهَا بِيَدِي وَسَهِرْتُ مَعَهَا نِصْفَ لَيْلَةٍ كَامِلَةٍ وَأَنَا أَتَفَرَّجُ عَلَى حُسْنِهَا وَجَمَالِهَا وَظَرْفِهَا وَدَلَالِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni yā ayyuhā al-shaykhu al-naḥsu a-taẓunnu annī raʾaytuhā bi-udhunī innamā raʾaytuhā bi-ʿuyūnī fī al-yaqaẓati wa-qallabtuhā bi-yadī wa-sahirtu maʿahā niṣfa laylatin kāmilatin wa-anā atafarraju ʿalā ḥusnihā wa-jamālihā wa-ẓarfihā wa-dalālihā
sentences.l: So-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: O you, the-old-man the-ill-omened, do-you-think that-I saw-her with-my-ear? Only I-saw-her with-my-eyes in the-waking, and-I-turned-her-over with-my-hand, and-I-stayed-awake with-her half (of) a-night complete, and-I gazing at her-beauty and-her-loveliness and-her-grace and-her-coquetry.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “You ill-omened old man, do you think I saw her with my ears? I saw her with my own eyes, wide awake. I turned her this way and that with my hand, and lay awake with her a full half of the night, feasting my eyes on her beauty and loveliness, her grace and her coquettish ways.
sentences.n: yā ayyuhā, “O you”, the two vocative words together. a-taẓunnu, “do you think?”, with the question particle a-; the shadda of اتظنّ is printed. bi-udhunī, “with my ear”, is his scornful answer to bi-ʿaynika, “with your eye”: how else would one see? bi-ʿuyūnī, “with my eyes”, uses the plural ʿuyūn for a pair of eyes, as speech often does; bi- of the instrument. qallabtuhā, Form II, “I turned her over and over”, handling her as one looks a thing over; qalabtuhā, Form I, is also possible from the letters, with much the same sense. sahira, “to stay awake at night”. tafarraja ʿalā, Form V, “to gaze at, look one's fill at”, a later usage. ẓarf, “grace, elegance”; dalāl, “coquetry, a beloved's teasing airs”: the four nouns go in two rhyming pairs.

sentences.t: وَإِنَّمَا أَنْتُمْ قَدْ عَلَّمْتُمُوهَا وَأَوْصَيْتُمُوهَا أَنَّهَا لَا تُكَلِّمُنِي فَجَعَلَتْ رُوحَهَا نَائِمَةً فَنِمْتُ بِجَانِبِهَا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ فَتَنَبَّهْتُ مِنْ مَنَامِي فَلَمْ أَجِدْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-innamā antum qad ʿallamtumūhā wa-awṣaytumūhā annahā lā tukallimunī fa-jaʿalat rūḥahā nāʾimatan fa-nimtu bi-jānibihā ilā al-ṣabāḥi fa-tanabbahtu min manāmī fa-lam ajidhā
sentences.l: But-only you (pl.) have taught-her and-instructed-her that-she not speak-to-me, so-she-made her-soul sleeping; and-I-slept at-her-side until the-morning, and-I-woke from my-sleep and-not I-found-her.
sentences.i: It is you, and no one else, who coached her and told her not to speak to me, and so she made out that she was asleep. I slept beside her until morning, and when I woke from my sleep I could not find her.”
sentences.n: wa-innamā antum, “but it is only you”: innamā puts the weight on the word after it. awṣā, Form IV, “to charge, instruct”, here followed by annahā and a plain imperfect, “that she should not speak to me”, where Classical Arabic would use an with the subjunctive: the same later construction as kallafa annahu in the last night. The shaddas of علّمتموها and فتنبّهت are printed. jaʿalat rūḥahā nāʾimatan, “she made her soul sleeping”: rūḥ with a suffix is the later reflexive, “herself”, and jaʿala with two objects here means “to make out, feign”. tanabbaha, Form V, “to wake”. lam ajidhā, jussive of wajada, “I did not find her”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ يَاسَيِّدِي قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ رُبَّمَا تَكُونُ أَنْتَ رَأَيْتَ هٰذَا الْأَمْرَ فِى الْمَنَامِ فَيَكُونُ أَضْغَاثَ أَحْلَامٍ أَوْ تَخَيُّلَاتٍ مِنْ أَكْلِ مُخْتَلِفِ الطَّعَامِ أَوْ وَسْوَسَةً مِنَ الشَّيَاطِينِ اللِّئَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru yā sayyidī Qamara al-Zamāni rubbamā takūnu anta raʾayta hādhā al-amra fī al-manāmi fa-yakūnu aḍghātha aḥlāmin aw takhayyulātin min akli mukhtalifi al-ṭaʿāmi aw waswasatan mina al-shayāṭīni al-liʾāmi
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-vizier: O-my-master Qamar al-Zamān, perhaps you-are, you, (that) you-saw this the-matter in the-sleep, so-it-is bundles (of) dreams, or imaginings from eating (of) varied the-food, or a-whispering from the-devils the-base.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “My master Qamar al-Zamān, perhaps you saw this thing in your sleep, and it is a jumble of dreams, or fancies that come of eating many kinds of food, or the whispering of the base devils.”
sentences.n: The print has اضعاث, a misprint for اضغاث, corrected here: aḍghāth aḥlām, “a jumble of dreams”, the Qurʾanic phrase (Yūsuf 12:44), which the print gives correctly two lines below. rubbamā takūnu anta raʾayta, “perhaps it is that you saw”: takūnu with a perfect is a later way of saying “you may have seen”. fa-yakūnu aḍghātha: the predicate of yakūnu stands in the accusative, and so do takhayyulātin (the feminine plural takes -in for the accusative) and waswasatan. mukhtalif al-ṭaʿām, “varied of food”, a mixed and heavy meal, thought to bring bad dreams. waswasa, “whispering”, the devil's prompting in the heart. The vizier drops into rhymed prose, al-ṭaʿām, al-liʾām; the ئ of اللئام is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَا أَيُّهَا الشَّيْخُ النَّحْسُ كَيْفَ تَهْزَأُبِي أَنْتَ الْآخَرُ وَتَقُولُ لِي لَعَلَّ هٰذَا أَضْغَاثُ أَحْلَامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni yā ayyuhā al-shaykhu al-naḥsu kayfa tahzaʾu bī anta al-ākharu wa-taqūlu lī laʿalla hādhā aḍghāthu aḥlāmin
sentences.l: So-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: O you, the-old-man the-ill-omened, how (do) you-mock with-me, you the-other, and-you-say to-me: Perhaps this (is) bundles (of) dreams,
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “You ill-omened old man, how can you mock me too, and tell me that perhaps this was a jumble of dreams,
sentences.n: The print runs تهزأ and بي together, تهزأبي, with its hamza printed; the spacing is kept. hazaʾa bi-, “to mock”: the verb takes its object with bi-. anta al-ākharu, “you too, you as well”, literally “you, the other one”, a later idiom. laʿalla, “perhaps”: its noun, hādhā, takes the place of an accusative, and its predicate, aḍghāthu, is nominative. The shadda of لعلّ is printed.

sentences.t: مَعَ أَنَّ هٰذَا الْخَادِمَ كَانَ قَدْ أَقَرَّ لِي بِتِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةِ وَقَالَ لِي فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ أَعُودُ إِلَيْكَ وَأُخْبِرُكَ بِقِصَّتِهَا
sentences.tr: maʿa anna hādhā al-khādima kāna qad aqarra lī bi-tilka al-ṣabiyyati wa-qāla lī fī hādhihi al-sāʿati aʿūdu ilayka wa-ukhbiruka bi-qiṣṣatihā
sentences.l: with that this the-servant had already confessed to-me with-that the-girl, and-said to-me: In this the-hour I-return to-you and-tell-you with-her-story?
sentences.i: when this servant had already owned to me that there was such a girl, and told me, ‘I will come back to you this very hour and tell you her story’?”
sentences.n: maʿa anna, “although, when in fact”. kāna qad aqarra, “had confessed”: kāna with qad and a perfect gives the pluperfect. aqarra bi-, Form IV, “to admit, own to”: the verb takes the thing admitted with bi-, here the girl herself, and li- marks the one the admission is made to. aʿūdu, the plain imperfect for the future, “I will come back”. The servant had not said quite this: half-drowned in the well, he promised to come back and tell the truth. The shaddas of اقرّ, الصبيّة and بقصّتها are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ قَامَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ وَتَقَدَّمَ إِلَى الْوَزِيرِ وَقَبَضَ لِحْيَتَهُ فِي يَدِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni qāma min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi wa-taqaddama ilā al-wazīri wa-qabaḍa liḥyatahu fī yadihi
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān rose from his-time and-his-hour, and-stepped-forward to the-vizier, and-grasped his-beard in his-hand.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān rose that very instant, went up to the vizier, and seized his beard in his hand.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”, the narrator's way of opening a new move: inna only marks the start of the statement and puts its subject in the accusative. min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi, “from his time and his hour”, the stock phrase for “at once”. taqaddama ilā, Form V, “to step up to”; its shadda is printed. qabaḍa, “to grasp, seize”, here with a direct object, the beard; qabaḍa ʿalā is the usual phrase for laying hold of a person.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ لِحْيَتُهُ طَوِيلَةً فَأَخَذَهَا قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَلَفَّهَا عَلَى يَدِهِ وَجَذَبَهُ مِنْهَا فَرَمَاةُ مِنْ فَوْقِ السَّرِيرِ وَأَلْقَاهُ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat liḥyatuhu ṭawīlatan fa-akhadhahā Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-laffahā ʿalā yadihi wa-jadhabahu minhā fa-ramāhu min fawqi al-sarīri wa-alqāhu ʿalā al-arḍi
sentences.l: And-was his-beard long; so-took-it Qamar al-Zamān and-wound-it on his-hand, and-pulled-him by-it, and-threw-him from on-top-of the-couch and-cast-him on the-ground.
sentences.i: Now the vizier's beard was long, and Qamar al-Zamān took hold of it, twisted it round his hand and dragged him by it, flinging him off the couch and down on the floor.
sentences.n: laffa ʿalā, “to wind round”; its shadda is printed. jadhabahu minhā, “he pulled him by it”: min marks the part he was pulled by. The print writes فرماة, with ة for the pronoun ه, as it does now and then: read fa-ramāhu, “and he threw him”. alqā, Form IV, “to cast down”. min fawqi al-sarīri, “from on top of the couch”, where the two had been sitting.

sentences.t: فَحَسَّ الْوَزِيرُ أَنَّ رُوحَهُ طَلَعَتْ مِنْ شِدَّةِ نَتْفِ لِحْيَتِهِ وَلَا زَالَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يَرْفُصُ الْوَزِيرَ بِرِجْلَيْهِ وَيَلْكُمُهُ فِي صَدْرِهِ وَعَلَى أَضْلَاعِهِ وَيَصْفَعُهُ عَلَى قَفَاهُ بِيَدَيْهِ حَتَّى كَادَ أَنْ يُهْلِكَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥassa al-wazīru anna rūḥahu ṭalaʿat min shiddati natfi liḥyatihi wa-lā zāla Qamaru al-Zamāni yarfuṣu al-wazīra bi-rijlayhi wa-yalkumuhu fī ṣadrihi wa-ʿalā aḍlāʿihi wa-yaṣfaʿuhu ʿalā qafāhu bi-yadayhi ḥattā kāda an yuhlikahu
sentences.l: And-felt the-vizier that his-soul had-gone-out from (the) severity (of the) plucking (of) his-beard; and-not ceased Qamar al-Zamān kicking the-vizier with-his-two-feet, and-punching-him in his-chest and-on his-ribs, and-slapping-him on his-nape with-his-two-hands, until he-was-about that he-destroy-him.
sentences.i: The vizier felt his soul leave him, so cruelly was his beard being torn; and Qamar al-Zamān went on kicking him and punching him in the chest and the ribs, and slapping him on the back of the neck with both hands, until he had all but killed him.
sentences.n: ḥassa, “to feel”, the later form of Classical aḥassa; its shadda is printed. ṭalaʿat rūḥuhu, “his soul came out”, the later idiom for being at death's door. natf, “plucking, tearing out” of hair. lā zāla with an imperfect, “he kept on doing”: in Classical Arabic lā zāla is mostly a wish, “may he never cease”, and the story-telling form is mā zāla or lam yazal; here it simply narrates. يرفص is rafasa, “to kick”, spelled with ṣ for s as in later speech, and read yarfuṣu. lakama, “to punch”; ṣafaʿa, “to slap”; qafā, “the nape”: a slap on the back of the neck is the classic humiliation. bi-rijlayhi and bi-yadayhi, duals with bi- of the instrument. kāda an, “was about to”: kāda usually takes the bare imperfect, but the an is found.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِذَا كَانَ الْعَبْدُ الْخَادِمُ خَلَّصَ نَفْسَهُ مِنْ هٰذَا الصَّبِيِّ الْمَجْنُونِ بِكَذِبِهِ فَأَنَا أَوْلَى بِذٰلِكَ مِنْهُ وَأُخَلِّصُ نَفْسِي أَنَا الْآخَرُ بِكَذْبَةٍ وَإِلَّا يُهْلِكُنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru fī nafsihi idhā kāna al-ʿabdu al-khādimu khallaṣa nafsahu min hādhā al-ṣabiyyi al-majnūni bi-kadhibihi fa-anā awlā bi-dhālika minhu wa-ukhalliṣu nafsī anā al-ākharu bi-kadhbatin wa-illā yuhlikunī
sentences.l: So-said the-vizier in himself: If was the-slave the-servant (that he) saved himself from this the-boy the-mad by-his-lie, then-I (am) more-worthy of-that than-he; and-I-will-save myself, I the-other, with-a-lie, or-else he-destroys-me.
sentences.i: The vizier said to himself, “If the slave who serves him could save himself from this mad boy with a lie, I have the better claim to do so. I too will save myself with a lie, or else he will kill me.
sentences.n: fī nafsihi, “in himself”, that is, silently, to himself. idhā kāna … khallaṣa, “if it is so that he saved”: kāna with a perfect sets the condition in the past. al-ʿabd al-khādim, “the slave, the servant”: the two words for the same man now stand together. khallaṣa, Form II, “to deliver, save”. bi-kadhibihi, “by his lying”: bi- of the means; kadhba below is “a single lie”. awlā bi-, “more entitled to”: bi- marks what one has the better right to, and min the one compared. anā al-ākharu, “I too”, as above. wa-illā, “or else”, from wa-in lā, “and if not”; Classical Arabic would put the verb after it in the jussive, yuhliknī, but it is vocalised here as a plain imperfect, yuhlikunī, as later speech has it. The shadda of والّا is printed.

sentences.t: فَهَا أَنَا أَكْذِبُ وَأُخَلِّصُ نَفْسِي مِنْهُ فَإِنَّهُ مَجْنُونٌ لَاشَكَّ فِي جُنُونِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-hā anā akdhibu wa-ukhalliṣu nafsī minhu fa-innahu majnūnun lā shakka fī junūnihi
sentences.l: So-here I (am): I-lie and-save myself from-him, for-indeed-he (is) mad, no doubt in his-madness.
sentences.i: So here I go: I will lie and save myself from him, for he is mad, and there is no doubt of his madness.”
sentences.n: hā anā, “here I am”, with an imperfect, “here I am, about to”, a lively turn of speech. The print runs لا and شك together, لاشكّ, with its shadda printed; the spacing is kept. lā shakka, the lā of total denial with the accusative, “there is no doubt”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْوَزِيرَ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِى لَا تُؤَاخِذْنِي فَإِنَّ وَالِدَكَ قَدْأَوْصَانِي أَنِّي أَكْتُمُ عَنْكَ خَبَرَ هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-wazīra iltafata ilā Qamari al-Zamāni wa-qāla lahu yā sayyidī lā tuʾākhidhnī fa-inna wālidaka qad awṣānī annī aktumu ʿanka khabara hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati
sentences.l: Then indeed the-vizier turned to Qamar al-Zamān and-said to-him: O my-master, not take-me-to-task, for indeed your-father has charged-me that-I hide from-you (the) news (of) this the-girl.
sentences.i: Then the vizier turned to Qamar al-Zamān and said to him, “My master, do not hold it against me: your father charged me to keep the story of this girl from you.
sentences.n: iltafata ilā, Form VIII, “to turn towards”. lā tuʾākhidhnī, “do not blame me, do not take me to task”, lā with the jussive of Form III ākhadha; the ؤ is printed, and so is the ى of سيدى. The print runs قد and اوصاني together, قداوصاني, read qad awṣānī, “he has charged me”; the spacing is kept. awṣā annī aktumu, “charged me that I should hide”, again anna with a plain imperfect. katama ʿan, “to hide from”. The vizier is now lying, as he has just told himself he would.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا الْآنَ عَجَزْتُ وَكَلَّيْتُ وَتَأَلَّمْتُ مِنَ الضَّرْبِ لِأَنِّي رَجُلٌ كَبِيرٌ وَلَيْسَ لِي جَلَدٌ وَلَاقُوَّةٌ عَلَى تَحَمُّلِ الضَّرْبِ
sentences.tr: wa-anā al-āna ʿajaztu wa-kallaytu wa-taʾallamtu mina al-ḍarbi li-annī rajulun kabīrun wa-laysa lī jaladun wa-lā quwwatun ʿalā taḥammuli al-ḍarbi
sentences.l: And-I now, I-have-become-powerless and-I-have-become-weary and-I-am-in-pain from the-beating, because-I (am) a-man old, and-not-is to-me endurance nor strength for bearing the-beating.
sentences.i: And now I am spent and worn out and aching from the blows, for I am an old man, and I have neither the endurance nor the strength to bear a beating.
sentences.n: The hamza and madda of الآن are printed. ʿajaza, “to be powerless, unable”, here “to be at the end of one's strength”. كلّيت, with its shadda printed, is read kallaytu, “I have grown weary”: the doubled verb kalla, whose Classical perfect is kalaltu, is treated in later speech as if its last letter were weak. taʾallama, Form V, “to feel pain”; the print gives its shadda but no hamza, وتالّمت. rajul kabīr, “a big man”, here means an old one. laysa lī, “there is not to me”: li- of possession. The print runs ولا and قوة together, ولاقوة; the spacing is kept. ʿalā taḥammuli, “for bearing”: ʿalā after strength marks what it is strength for.

sentences.t: فَتَمَهَّلْ عَلَيَّ قَلِيلًا حَتَّى أُحَدِّ ثَكَ وَأُخْبِرَكَ بِقِصَّةِ الصَّبِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-tamahhal ʿalayya qalīlan ḥattā uḥaddithaka wa-ukhbiraka bi-qiṣṣati al-ṣabiyyati
sentences.l: So-go-slowly on-me a-little, until I-talk-to-you and-tell-you with-(the)-story (of) the-girl.
sentences.i: Bear with me a little, and I will tell you all about the girl.”
sentences.n: tamahhala ʿalā, Form V, “to go gently with”: ʿalā marks the one spared; the shaddas of فتمهّل and عليّ are printed. The print splits the word احدثك across a space, احد ثك; it is read as one, uḥaddithaka, “I tell you”, and the space is kept. ḥattā takes the subjunctive, uḥaddithaka and ukhbiraka: “so that I may tell you”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ مَاسَمِعَ مِنْهُ ذٰلِكَ بَطَّلَ عَنْهُ الضَّرْبَ وَقَالَ لَهُ لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ لَمْ تُخْبِرْنِي بِخَبَرِ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةِ إِلَّا بَعْدَ الْإِهَانَةِ وَالضَّرْبِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda mā samiʿa minhu dhālika baṭṭala ʿanhu al-ḍarba wa-qāla lahu li-ayyi shayʾin lam tukhbirnī bi-khabari tilka al-ṣabiyyati illā baʿda al-ihānati wa-al-ḍarbi
sentences.l: So-at what he-heard from-him that, he-stopped from-him the-beating, and-said to-him: For-what thing not you-told-me with-(the)-news (of) that the-girl except after the-humiliation and-the-beating?
sentences.i: When he heard this from him, he left off beating him and said to him, “Why would you not tell me about this girl until you had been shamed and beaten?
sentences.n: The print runs ما and سمع together, ماسمع; the spacing is kept. ʿinda mā, “when”: mā turns the verb into a clause after ʿinda. بطل is read baṭṭala, Form II, “to stop, leave off”, with al-ḍarb as its object, a later usage; one could also read baṭala ʿanhu al-ḍarbu, Form I, “the beating ceased from him”. li-ayyi shayʾin, “for what thing?”, that is, “why?”: li- gives the reason; the shadda of لايّ and the ء of شيء are printed. lam … illā baʿda, “not … except after”, that is, “only after”. ihāna, Form IV verbal noun, “humiliation, insult”. The shaddas of الصبيّة and الّا are printed.

sentences.t: فَقُمْ يَا أَيُّهَا الشَّيْخُ النَّحْسُ وَاحْكِ لِي عَنْ خَبَرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qum yā ayyuhā al-shaykhu al-naḥsu wa-iḥki lī ʿan khabarihā
sentences.l: So-rise, O you, the-old-man the-ill-omened, and-relate to-me about her-news.
sentences.i: Get up, you ill-omened old man, and tell me about her.”
sentences.n: iḥki, imperative of ḥakā, “to relate”, with its last vowel shortened; the kasra of احكِ is printed. ḥakā ʿan, “to tell about”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ هَلْ أَنْتَ تَسْأَلُ عَنْ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةِ صَاحِبَةِ الْوَجْهِ الْمَلِيحِ وَالْقَدِّ الرَّجِيحِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru hal anta tasʾalu ʿan tilka al-ṣabiyyati ṣāḥibati al-wajhi al-malīḥi wa-al-qaddi al-rajīḥi
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-vizier: (Is it that) you, you-ask about that the-girl, (the) owner (of) the-face the-lovely and-the-stature the-weighty?
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “Is it the girl you are asking about, she of the lovely face and the full, shapely figure?”
sentences.n: The vizier plays along, and buys his safety in rhymed prose: al-malīḥ, al-rajīḥ. qadd, “stature, figure”. rajīḥ, “weighty, outweighing”: of a figure it means full and well rounded, of a mind, as in the last night, sound. The hamza of تسأل is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ نَعَمْ أَخْبِرْنِي أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ مَنِ الَّذِي أَتَى بِهَا إِلَيَّ وَأَنَا مَهًا بِجَانِبِي وَمَنِ الَّذِي أَخَذَهَا مِنْ جَانِبِي فِى اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni naʿam akhbirnī ayyuhā al-wazīru mani alladhī atā bihā ilayya wa-anā mahan bi-jānibī wa-mani alladhī akhadhahā min jānibī fī al-layli
sentences.l: So-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: Yes. Tell-me, O vizier, who (is) the-one-who came with-her to-me, and-I, an-oryx (?) at-my-side, and-who (is) the-one-who took-her from my-side in the-night?
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “Yes. Tell me, vizier, who brought her to me while I lay with her at my side, and who took her from my side in the night?
sentences.n: atā bi-, “to bring”: the verb chooses bi-, “to come with”. The shadda of اليّ is printed: ilayya, “to me”. The words وانا مها بجانبي are doubtful. As printed, مها can only be mahan, “wild cows, oryxes”, the animal poets liken a lovely woman to for her large dark eyes, which would give something like “while I had my oryx at my side”; but that is strained, and more likely the compositor dropped a letter from معها, wa-anā maʿahā, “while I was with her”. The print is kept and vocalised mahan; the idiomatic line follows the likelier sense. mani alladhī, “who is it that”, with a helping -i on man before the joining alif.

sentences.t: وَأَيْنَ ذَهَبَتْ هِيَ فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ حَتَّى أَرُوحَ أَنَا إِلَيْهَا بِنَفْسِي
sentences.tr: wa-ayna dhahabat hiya fī hādhihi al-sāʿati ḥattā arūḥa anā ilayhā bi-nafsī
sentences.l: And-where went she in this the-hour, so-that I-go, I, to-her by-myself?
sentences.i: And where has she gone now, so that I may go to her myself?
sentences.n: ḥattā with the subjunctive, arūḥa, “so that I may go”. bi-nafsī, “myself, in person”: bi- with nafs puts the stress on the man himself. The pronouns hiya and anā are added for emphasis, as speech adds them.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ كَانَ أَبِي الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ فَعَلَ مَعِي هٰذِهِ الْفِعَالَ وَامْتَحَنَنِي بِتِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةِ الْمَلِيحَةِ مِنْ أَجْلِ زَوَاجِهَا فَأَنَا رَضِيتُ أَنْ أَتَزَوَّجَ بِهَا وَأُرِيحَ نَفْسِي مِنْ هٰذَا
sentences.tr: fa-in kāna abī al-maliku Shahramānu faʿala maʿī hādhihi al-fiʿāla wa-imtaḥananī bi-tilka al-ṣabiyyati al-malīḥati min ajli zawājihā fa-anā raḍītu an atazawwaja bihā wa-urīḥa nafsī min hādhā
sentences.l: So-if was my-father the-King Shahramān (that he) did with-me these the-deeds and-tested-me with-that the-girl the-lovely for (the) sake (of) her-marrying, then-I have-consented that I-marry with-her and-give-rest (to) myself from this.
sentences.i: If it was my father, King Shahramān, who did all this to me, and put me to the test with that lovely girl so that I would marry her, then I consent to marry her and spare myself all this.
sentences.n: in kāna … faʿala, “if it is so that he did”: kāna with a perfect in a condition about the past, as with idhā kāna above. faʿala maʿa, “to do (something) to”, the later idiom. imtaḥana bi-, Form VIII, “to test with”: bi- marks the means of the test. min ajli, “for the sake of”. raḍītu, “I consent”, the perfect for a decision made there and then; the ḍamma of رضيتُ is printed. tazawwaja bi-, “to marry”: the later language puts the bride after bi-, where Classical Arabic says tazawwajahā. arāḥa nafsahu min, Form IV, “to give oneself rest from”, here urīḥa, subjunctive after an.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ مَافَعَلَ مَعِي هٰذَا الْأَ مْرَكُلَّهُ إِلَّا مِنْ أَجْلِ امْتِنَاعِي مِنَ الزَّوَاجِ
sentences.tr: fa-innahu mā faʿala maʿī hādhā al-amra kullahu illā min ajli imtināʿī mina al-zawāji
sentences.l: For-indeed-he not did with-me this the-matter all-of-it except for (the) sake (of) my-refusing from the-marriage.
sentences.i: For he has done all this to me only because I refused to marry.
sentences.n: The print runs ما and فعل together, مافعل; the spacing is kept. Here mā is the negative: mā … illā, “he did not do … except”, that is, “he did it only”. The print also sets الا مركلّه, with the space in the wrong place: the words are al-amra kullahu, “the whole matter, all of it”. The spacing is kept and the vowels are put on the letters where they stand. The shaddas of مركلّه and الّا are printed. imtanaʿa min, Form VIII, “to refuse, hold back from”: it was the prince's long refusal of marriage that began all this.

sentences.t: فَهَا أَنَا رَضِيتُ بِالزَّوَاجِ ثُمَّ رَضِيتُ بِالزَّوَاجِ
sentences.tr: fa-hā anā raḍītu bi-al-zawāji thumma raḍītu bi-al-zawāji
sentences.l: So-here I (am): I-have-consented to-the-marriage, then I-have-consented to-the-marriage.
sentences.i: See, I consent to marry; I say it again, I consent to marry.
sentences.n: raḍiya bi-, “to be content with, accept”: the verb takes what is accepted with bi-. The repetition with thumma, “and then again”, is for emphasis, as a man says a thing twice to bind himself.

sentences.t: فَأَعْلِمْ وَالِدِي بِذٰلِكَ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ وَأَشِرْ إِلَيْهِ أَنْ يُزَوِّجَنِي بِتِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةِ فَإِنِّي لَاأُرِيدُ سِوَاهَا وَقَلْبِي لَايُحِبُّ إِلَّا إِيَّاهَا
sentences.tr: fa-aʿlim wālidī bi-dhālika ayyuhā al-wazīru wa-ashir ilayhi an yuzawwijanī bi-tilka al-ṣabiyyati fa-innī lā urīdu siwāhā wa-qalbī lā yuḥibbu illā iyyāhā
sentences.l: So-inform my-father of-that, O vizier, and-point to-him that he-marry-me with that the-girl; for-indeed-I not want other-than-her, and-my-heart not loves except her.
sentences.i: So tell my father of this, vizier, and put it to him that he should marry me to that girl; for I want no one but her, and my heart loves none but her.
sentences.n: aʿlim, Form IV imperative, “inform”; aʿlama bi-, “to inform of”: bi- marks what is made known. ashir, imperative of ashāra, Form IV, “to point, signal”; ashāra ilā here means “to put it to, propose to”, where Classical Arabic says ashāra ʿalā for “to advise”. zawwaja bi-, Form II, “to marry (someone) to”: bi- marks the bride, as with tazawwaja bi-. The print runs لا and اريد, and لا and يحبّ, together, لااريد and لايحبّ, the second with its shadda printed; the spacing is kept. illā iyyāhā, “none but her”: when illā parts the object from its verb, the pronoun is carried by iyyā-; the shadda of الّا is printed.

sentences.t: فَقُمْ وَأَسْرِعْ إِلَى أَبِي وَأَشِرْ إِلَيْهِ بِتَعْجِيلِ زَوَاجِي ثُمَّ عُدْ إِنِّي بِالْجَوَابِ فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qum wa-asriʿ ilā abī wa-ashir ilayhi bi-taʿjīli zawājī thumma ʿud innī bi-al-jawābi fī hādhihi al-sāʿati
sentences.l: So-rise and-hurry to my-father and-point to-him with-(the)-hastening (of) my-marriage; then return, indeed-I (?) with-the-answer, in this the-hour.
sentences.i: Up, then, hurry to my father and urge him to hasten my marriage, and come back to me with the answer this very hour.”
sentences.n: ashāra bi-, “to advise, recommend (something)”: bi- marks what is proposed, here taʿjīl, “hastening”, the verbal noun of Form II ʿajjala. The words عد انّي are doubtful. As printed, with its shadda, انّي is innī, “indeed I”, which gives no clear sense: “return; indeed I … with the answer”. The sense wants ʿud ilayya, “come back to me”, and the print may have slipped for اليّ; but the letters and the printed shadda both point to innī, so the print is kept and vocalised as it stands, and the idiomatic line gives the likely sense. bi-al-jawābi, “with the answer”: bi- of what one comes back bringing.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ نَعَمْ وَمَا صَدَّقَ أَنَّهُ يَخْلُصُ مِنْ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru naʿam wa-mā ṣaddaqa annahu yakhluṣu min yadayhi
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-vizier: Yes; and-not he-believed that-he gets-free from his-two-hands.
sentences.i: “Yes,” the vizier said to him, scarcely able to believe he was getting out of his hands.
sentences.n: mā ṣaddaqa anna, “he did not believe that”, the later idiom for “he could hardly believe that”, said of a narrow escape. khalaṣa min, “to get free of”. yadayhi, “his two hands”, the dual.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ وَخَرَجَ مِنَ الْبُرْجِ هُوَ يَمْشِي وَيَعْثُرُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْخَوْفِ وَالْفَزَعِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يَجْرِي إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَ عَلَى الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma min ʿindihi wa-kharaja mina al-burji huwa yamshī wa-yaʿthuru min shiddati al-khawfi wa-al-fazaʿi wa-lam yazal yajrī ilā an dakhala ʿalā al-maliki Shahramāna
sentences.l: Then he-rose from with-him and-went-out from the-tower, he walking and-stumbling from (the) severity (of) the-fear and-the-fright; and-not he-ceased running until that he-entered upon the-King Shahramān.
sentences.i: Then he rose and left him, and went out of the tower, walking and stumbling for very fear and fright, and ran on without stopping until he came in to King Shahramān.
sentences.n: qāma min ʿindihi, “he rose from beside him”, that is, he took his leave. huwa yamshī, “he walking”, a clause of state without the wāw that Classical Arabic would usually set before it, wa-huwa yamshī. ʿathara, “to stumble”. lam yazal with an imperfect, “he kept on”, and ilā an with a perfect, “until”: the very words that carried the servant to the king in the last night. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (a person)”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
